children.text: TB-500 is the synthetic analog of Thymosin Beta-4, a naturally occurring peptide found in virtually every human and animal cell. Greenstone Wellness offers it at 10mg/mL — a higher-concentration formulation designed for research contexts where precision and volume efficiency matter. This post covers what's inside the vial, why concentration matters in peptide research, and what the published literature shows about TB-500's mechanisms.
What Is TB-500?

Thymosin Beta-4 (Tβ4) is a 43-amino-acid peptide encoded by the TMSB4X gene. It plays a central regulatory role in actin dynamics — the cellular machinery that governs how tissues grow, migrate, and repair. TB-500 is the synthetic form of the active fragment of this peptide, and it has become one of the most studied compounds in regenerative biology research over the past two decades.
Preclinical research has focused primarily on its role in several interconnected areas:
Wound healing and tissue repair
Angiogenesis — the formation of new blood vessels
Inflammation modulation during the repair process
Muscle fiber recruitment and recovery signaling
Why 10mg/mL? The Case for Higher Concentration

Standard TB-500 formulations are typically available as lyophilized powder at 5mg, or in solution at lower concentration profiles. Greenstone's 10mg/mL vial delivers twice the peptide content per milliliter compared to the standard 5mg/mL offering — same volume footprint, significantly higher precision ceiling.
For research purposes, this has practical implications:
Precision:
Higher concentration means smaller volumes per measured amount, which reduces measurement variability in experimental protocols.
Efficiency:
Researchers working with consistent administration windows can use less carrier volume while maintaining equivalent peptide content.
Stability:
When properly stored at 2–8°C and shielded from light, concentrated TB-500 solutions maintain structural integrity across their labeled shelf life.
The 10mg/mL formulation is not intended to encourage higher-dose protocols. It's engineered for precision and flexibility within existing research parameters.

What the Research Shows

The bulk of published TB-500 research has investigated its role in tissue regeneration — specifically cardiac tissue, tendon repair, and wound healing models. A 2010 study in the Journal of Molecular Medicine found that Tβ4 promoted cardiac repair following myocardial infarction in animal models by stimulating cardiomyocyte and endothelial progenitor cell migration. Research published in the Annals of the New York Academy of Sciences highlighted Tβ4's role in corneal and skin wound repair, noting accelerated healing timelines in treated subjects.

Multiple preclinical studies have documented its effect on reducing local inflammation while preserving regenerative signaling — a mechanism distinct from conventional anti-inflammatory approaches. It's worth noting that most of this body of research is preclinical. Human trials remain limited, and no approved therapeutic uses currently exist in the United States for TB-500.
